items.a: Do I need a panel upgrade before solar?
items.b: Often, yes. The array has to interconnect somewhere with capacity to spare. We assess the service first so the answer arrives before you sign, not during the install.

items.a: Do you repair solar you did not install?
items.b: Yes. Inverter faults, dead strings, monitoring dropouts and post-storm checks. It is a common call when the original installer has gone.

items.a: Is a permit required for solar in Chicago?
items.b: Yes, and solar is one of the highest-volume permitted categories in the city. We pull and close it in-house.

items.a: How long does interconnection take with ComEd?
items.b: Utility timelines vary and sit outside our control, which is exactly why we schedule around them rather than promising a date we cannot hold.

items.a: Does solar work on a Chicago flat roof?
items.b: Yes — ballasted or attached racking depending on the roof and the structure. Flat roofs are common here and are not an obstacle.

items.a: Should I replace my roof before installing solar?
items.b: If the roof has only a few years left, usually yes. Removing and reinstalling an array later adds cost. We check roof condition at the assessment and tell you if the roof should come first.

items.a: Will my solar panels work during a power outage?
items.b: Not on their own. A grid-tied array shuts off in an outage, so it can't feed power into lines utility crews are working on. To keep power you need a battery, or a backup-capable inverter, set up to run the circuits you choose.

items.a: Can I put solar on a two-flat or a condo building?
items.b: Yes, but the questions change. On a two-flat or three-flat we settle which meter the array connects to. In a condo building the roof is usually a common element, so the association's approval comes before design.

items.a: My installer went out of business. Who handles the warranty?
items.b: Equipment warranties usually sit with the manufacturer, not the installer, so they can still apply. A closed installer's workmanship warranty usually can't be claimed. We can diagnose the fault and give you what the manufacturer asks for.

items.a: How many visits does a solar installation take?
items.b: At least an assessment, the installation and the inspection. Panel or service work, a battery, or waiting on ComEd can add visits. The written scope lists the visits we expect.

An array feeds power back through your panel. Electrical code caps how much it can feed, based on the panel's busbar rating and the size of its main breaker. A panel that is already full, or has a small busbar, may not have room even when it seems fine for everyday use. There are three ways around that: connect on the supply side of the main breaker, replace the panel with one that has a larger busbar, or upgrade the service. Which one fits depends on the panel, the meter arrangement and the building.

items.a: Why older Chicago buildings change the job
items.b: Much of the north and northwest side predates 1940. Those buildings were wired for lighting and have had loads added ever since, so 100A services and crowded panels are common. Brick walls lengthen conduit routes. Two-flats raise the question of which meter the array serves, and converted condos need association approval for the shared roof.

items.a: How the City and ComEd steps fit together
items.b: The City issues the permit and inspects the work. ComEd approves the interconnection and grants approval to operate. Both have their own timelines, and the system stays off until both are done. That is why we schedule around them rather than promise a date we can't hold.

Equipment warranties usually sit with the manufacturer, so they can outlive the installer. Diagnosis comes first: the symptom points to where to look, and the error code and monitoring history narrow it down. If a part is discontinued, the replacement can change the wiring, and we tell you that before quoting.

items.b: Inverters usually need attention long before the panels do. The make, model and operating conditions decide the actual life, so we read the error history before recommending a replacement.

items.a: Can I add a battery to my existing inverter?
items.b: Sometimes. It depends on the inverter model. Hybrid inverters are built for it; others need an AC-coupled battery. We check before recommending equipment.

items.a: Why does my inverter keep shutting off?
items.b: Common causes are grid voltage at the edge of its range, a loose connection or overheating. The error log usually tells us which.

items.a: Will my inverter work during a power outage?
items.b: Not on its own. A grid-tied inverter shuts off when the grid goes down so it can't feed lines crews are working on. Backup needs a battery and a backup-capable setup.

items.a: My installer went out of business. Who handles the warranty?
items.b: Equipment warranties usually sit with the manufacturer, so they can still apply. We can diagnose the fault and give you what the manufacturer asks for.

Panels are passive and sealed. The inverter converts power all day, runs hot and is full of electronics, so it is usually the first component to need attention.

A dead inverter usually means a working array that cannot deliver power, not a failed system.

An inverter feeds power back through your panel. Code caps how much it can feed, based on the panel's busbar rating and main breaker. A full or small panel may not have room, which is why a panel or service upgrade sometimes comes first.

If your model is discontinued, the replacement may be a different type. Microinverters add equipment under every panel; a hybrid inverter prepares the system for a battery. Each changes the wiring, the price and sometimes the permit route.

Systems installed years ago may not have the disconnects, labels or rapid shutdown that current rules expect. When we replace the inverter we tell you what the inspector will look for, before the work starts.
